title: NGC 7090: An actively star-forming galaxy
caption: The edge-on spiral galaxy NGC 7090, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: We see the galaxy NGC 7090 edge-on in this Hubble image, so its spiral arms are hard to make out. Instead, its disc and bulging central core are on show, with an intricate pattern of pinkish-red patches spread across the whole galaxy and dark dust lanes inside the disc.
The pink regions are clouds of hydrogen gas, and they mark places where stars are forming right now. They offer visual confirmation of studies that class NGC 7090 as an actively star-forming galaxy.

The dark lanes are dust, mostly in the lower half, with a fine, threadlike structure. Looking through the whole disc from outside, the dust soaks up light from the bright centre and stands out in silhouette. Dust like this is a long-standing obstacle for astronomers, but near-infrared light passes through it largely unhindered, and radio telescopes can observe the dust itself.

understand.summary: This image comes from the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. Orange light is coloured blue, infrared is coloured red, and the glow of hydrogen gas is also shown in red.
understand.eye: The colours are shifted from what the eye would see, and part of the data is infrared light, invisible to us.

explore: NGC 7090 lies in the southern constellation Indus, the Indian, about thirty million light-years from the Sun according to the caption. John Herschel first observed it on 4 October 1834.
A version of this image was entered into Hubble's Hidden Treasures competition by Rasid Tugral.
alt: An edge-on spiral galaxy with a bright central bulge, pinkish-red patches across its disc and dark filamentary dust lanes in its lower half.
